title: The Architecture of Silence: Mapping Semantic Interruptions
content: A chatbot answers "Resolved". The report has been registered and passed on; the danger remains unaddressed. Meaning can stop short of a decision, even amid lively exchange. We call these places semantic interruptions and the conditions under which they accumulate and recur the architecture of silence. This conceptual article, grounded empirically in open materials, asks which functions a word must perform for knowledge to pass between roles, where these functions are interrupted in technologically mediated interaction, and which practices restore the conversation. We draw on research on knowledge boundaries, organisational silence, contact infrastructure, interprofessional education and Gestalt theory to trace the path from word to meaning, decision, action and consequence. The model proposes eight working analytical functions, four forms of silence, modifications of contact between roles, compensation, cognitive debt and practices of restoration. We offer hypotheses, an instrument for comparing utterances and implications for development, education, scientific communication and suicide research. Crisis communication serves as our lens: where suicide risk is concerned, the price may be a human life. The model has yet to be tested on independent material. Whether large language models help us speak depends on the function they are assigned and on who checks the answer.
